ann_90.text: Through this part, more daytime minutes (112 to 249) clearly raise the typical customer's predicted chance of leaving steadily, from below 1% to about 17%, and an international plan clearly raises it from about 1% to about 16%.
More voice-mail messages slightly raise it steadily to about 6%, a higher international charge and more evening minutes steadily to about 3%, and a higher evening charge steadily to about 2%.
A voice-mail plan slightly lowers it to below 1% (on the training data only).

Compared with the states this part does not single out, California and Washington slightly raise it to about 5% to 6% and Montana, Maryland, South Carolina, Connecticut, Oregon, North Carolina and Kansas to about 2% to 3%, while Hawaii, Vermont and Colorado slightly lower it to below 1% and most of the other listed states to about 1% (on the training data only).

More night-time minutes, a longer account and more daytime calls slightly raise it steadily to about 2%, and more international minutes slightly lower it steadily to about 1% (on the training data only).
Area codes 510 and 408 slightly lower it to about 1%, and more night-time calls slightly lower it in an uneven way, to about 1% (on the training data only).

ann_91.text: Through this part, more daytime minutes clearly lower the predicted chance of leaving only while they stay below about 169 minutes (between 154 and 214 minutes for different customers), and in an uneven way across customers: for the typical customer, going from 91 to 352 minutes moves it from about 47% to about 1%.
Across the usual range (112 to 249 minutes), more daytime minutes clearly lower it in an uneven way across customers, from about 21% to about 1% through this part.

This part makes daytime minutes count for more when the evening charge is above 17.12 US dollars: across the whole model the predicted chance is lowest at about 154 minutes and higher either side, and going from 112 to 249 minutes clearly raises it from about 2% to about 20% for such customers, against about 4% to about 14% for the others.
It also makes daytime minutes count for less in South Dakota: from about 6% to about 11% there, against about 2% to about 17% in most states.

Customer-service calls (0 to 3) slightly raise it in an uneven way across customers, and even more so if the evening charge is 17.12 US dollars or less: from about 1% to about 6%, against about 2% either way otherwise.

A higher evening charge and a higher international charge slightly lower it in an uneven way across customers, the international charge only while it stays below about 2.96 US dollars (between 2.96 and 4.53 US dollars for different customers), and being in South Dakota slightly raises it while California, Arkansas and Utah slightly lower it (on the training data only).

ann_92.text: This part acts on 306 of 4000 customers, 154 of whom left; for the typical one (a customer in Idaho with 4 customer-service calls) it raises the predicted chance of leaving from about 16% to about 26% (on the training data only).
For that customer, being in West Virginia removes this rise: any other state gives about 26%, against about 16% in West Virginia (on the training data only).
For the typical customer, who is in West Virginia, calls add nothing until about 4 calls, then add to it steadily but only slightly, staying at about 1% (on the training data only).

ann_93.text: Through this part, a voice-mail plan slightly lowers the predicted chance of leaving, staying at about 1% for the typical customer (on the training data only).
Compared with West Virginia, being in any state other than Alabama slightly raises it to about 2%, while Alabama slightly lowers it, staying at about 1% (on the training data only).

ann_94.text: Through this part, being in Tennessee or Ohio slightly raises the predicted chance of leaving to about 2% (on the training data only).
Being in Nevada, California, Arizona, Missouri or Massachusetts slightly lowers it to about 1% (on the training data only).

ann_95.text: Across the whole model, an international plan clearly raises the typical customer's predicted chance of leaving from about 1% to about 16%.

Washington and California slightly raise it to about 6%, Montana to about 4% and Maryland, South Carolina, Tennessee, Connecticut, Ohio, Oregon and about a dozen other states to about 2% to 3%, while Hawaii and Vermont slightly lower it to below 1% and Colorado, Pennsylvania, Alaska, Virginia, Wyoming, Wisconsin, Alabama, Missouri and Nevada to about 1% (on the training data only).
More voice-mail messages (0 to 32) slightly raise it steadily to about 6%, and more evening minutes slightly raise it steadily to about 3%.
Customer-service calls (0 to 3) slightly raise it in an uneven way, to about 3%, and a voice-mail plan slightly lowers it to below 1%.
A higher international charge slightly raises it in an uneven way, to about 3% (on the training data only).

More night-time minutes, more daytime calls and a longer account slightly raise it steadily to about 2%, and more international minutes slightly lower it steadily to about 1% (on the training data only).
Area codes 510 and 408 slightly lower it to about 1%, and more night-time calls slightly lower it in an uneven way, to about 1% (on the training data only).
It ignores the daytime charge, evening calls, international calls and night-time charge.

ann_90.original: Hypothesis: a sparse logistic-regression term. identity_lin sums the 41 direct input->output edges: totalDayMinutes +2.02, voiceMailPlan -0.99, internationalPlan +0.75, totalIntlCharge +0.70, numberVmailMessages +0.61, totalEveMinutes +0.50 and totalEveCharge +0.35 (identical after z-scoring, so evening slope 0.85), totalNightMinutes +0.30, accountLength +0.13, totalDayCalls +0.12, and state offsets, the largest state:11 -0.30, state:46 -0.29, state:5 -0.20 (each one-hot z is about 7, so these are 1.4 to 2.2 logit offsets on 73-80 rows, roughly 2x the empirical log-odds). numberCustomerServiceCalls has no direct edge: CSC enters only through the hinges. Evidence: exact closed form; zeroing it drops train AUC to 0.54.
ann_90.proposed: A backbone of separate effects in which more daytime minutes (below 1% to about 17%) and an international plan (about 1% to 16%) raise the chance of leaving; voice-mail, usage, account and state effects are slight.

ann_91.original: Hypothesis: a low-usage hinge whose threshold rises with customer service calls (CSC). 807 = relu(-1.36 dayMin + 0.05 CSC + 0.69*2627 + 0.61*2796 - 1.30), where 2627 = 1.01 + 0.32 relu(0.87 CSC - 0.09) (always positive, affine in a CSC hinge) and 2796 = relu(0.41 - 1.00 eveCharge + 0.37 CSC + 0.15 state:41 + 0.34*12926), with 12926/13061 a two-stage CSC hinge that turns on at 3 calls. 1264 = relu(0.077 - 0.32 intlCharge + 0.39*807) adds 0.39*807 and a convex low-intl-charge hinge. Readout 1.59*807 + 1.81*1264 (252 is near dead, readout -2e-5, and holds a state:2/state:44/state:4 path). Evidence (train, n=4000): sensitivity of 807 is dayMin 0.63, eveCharge 0.22, CSC 0.20. Mean gate logit rises 1.1 -> 7.4 from 0 to 7 calls. With the backbone +2.02 dayMin, the logit is V-shaped in day minutes; for CSC>=4 the low-usage arm dominates (empirical churn 0.88 low-day vs 0.24 high-day, which the network reproduces). The same hinge also lifts low-CSC, very-low-day customers (93 rows, predicted 0.17 vs empirical 0.04): a mild overextension. totalEveCharge equals totalEveMinutes after z-scoring, so the gate effectively uses evening usage. Ablation: linearising this gate drops train AUC 0.901 -> 0.851; restoring it alone on the fully linearised model gives 0.836 -> 0.899. It is the source of nearly all of the network s gain over a linear model.
ann_91.proposed: A low-daytime-usage part: fewer daytime minutes raise the chance of leaving, steeply below about 169 minutes (between 154 minutes and 214 minutes for different customers) (about 47% to 1% from 91 to 352 minutes); it shapes how daytime minutes combine with the evening charge and makes customer-service calls count more at a low evening charge.

ann_92.original: Hypothesis: a service-call threshold switched off for one state. 7208 = relu(0.54 CSC - 0.37 state:49 - 0.68), readout +1.48. Active only when CSC >= 4 calls (7.6% of train rows), adding about 0.61 logit per extra call. For state:49 (one-hot z = 5.64) the pre-activation drops by 2.1, so the hinge is never active for state:49: 12 state:49 customers with CSC>=4 (5 churned, 42% vs 50% for other states) lose up to 2.75 logits. Evidence: closed form exact; linearising this unit costs only 0.002 AUC (0.901 -> 0.899) because csc_usage_gate already encodes CSC>=4. The state:49 exemption is a rare-category switch fitted to about 12 rows.
ann_92.proposed: A customer-service step acting on 306 customers, raising a typical such customer's chance of leaving from about 16% to 26%, switched off in West Virginia (on the training data only).

ann_93.original: Hypothesis: a linear voicemail-plan discount. 5577 = relu(0.98 voiceMailPlan + 0.25 state:1 + 1.0) -> 1133 = relu(0.14*5577 + 0.02 state:27 + 0.69) -> 4051 = relu(1.15*1133 + 0.06 state:49 + 2.10); readouts -0.88*1133 - 1.00*4051. All three ReLUs are active on every train row, so the chain is exactly linear on the data: net -0.29 logit per z of voiceMailPlan (on top of the backbone -0.99), -0.07 per z of state:1, -0.06 per z of state:49. Linearising it changes nothing (AUC 0.9009).
ann_93.proposed: A voice-mail discount with slight state adjustments; all effects are slight and seen on the training data only.

ann_94.original: Hypothesis: per-state logit offsets. Every unit reads one (or a few) state one-hots, so it is an exact function of binary inputs and hence a constant offset per state: 10249 (state:3, -0.009 readout), 11427 (state:42, +0.05), 14942 (state:35, +0.04), 161_a (state:4, -0.03), 6730 (constant +0.43 logit except state:33, where it switches off: -0.45 logit for 77 rows), 8896 (state:19, <0.001), 3861 (state:50, dead on all rows). Evidence: sensitivity analysis on train; linear fit R2 = 1.0; zeroing all of them leaves AUC unchanged (0.9009). The state:33 switch has the opposite sign to the data (empirical log-odds +0.33).
ann_94.proposed: Per-state adjustments for Tennessee, Ohio, Nevada, California, Arizona, Missouri and Massachusetts; all slight and seen on the training data only.

ann_95.original: Root: logit P(churn) = -1.068 + linear_backbone + 1.59*807 + 1.81*1264 + 1.48*7208 - 0.88*1133 - 1.00*4051 + state offsets (+ negligible 252), purely additive in logit; the sigmoid is the only coupling. 22 inputs are unconnected (incl. totalDayCharge, totalNightCharge, totalEveCalls, totalIntlCalls, areaCode:408, 16 states) and have zero effect. Train AUC 0.901, accuracy 0.906. Performance sources (train): all children replaced by least-squares linear fits gives AUC 0.836; restoring csc_usage_gate alone gives 0.899, csc_hinge_7208 alone 0.851, voicemail_chain and state_offsets alone 0.836 (they are exactly linear on binary inputs). So the extra AUC over linear comes from the CSC x low-usage gate. Rare-category switches: backbone state:11/46/5 offsets of -2.2/-2.1/-1.4 logits on 73-80 rows (empirical -1.2/-0.8/-0.5), state:49 disabling the CSC>=4 hinge for 12 rows, state:33 offset of the wrong sign.
ann_95.proposed: The model adds a backbone of separate effects, a low-daytime-usage part, a voice-mail part, a customer-service step and state adjustments; an international plan raises the chance of leaving from about 1% to 16%, other single effects are slight, and the daytime charge, evening calls, international calls and night-time charge are ignored.

summary.text: For a typical customer (one in West Virginia with area code 415, an account length of 100, no international or voice-mail plan, one customer-service call and median usage such as 180 daytime minutes), the model predicts about a 1% chance that the customer leaves, and an international plan clearly raises that to about 16%.

Daytime minutes work in two opposite directions: going from 112 to 249 minutes clearly lowers it, in an uneven way across customers, from about 21% to about 1% through one part, and clearly raises it steadily from below 1% to about 17% through another.

In the first of these parts, more daytime minutes clearly lower it only while they stay below about 169 minutes (between 154 and 214 minutes for different customers), and in an uneven way across customers: for the typical customer, going from 91 to 352 minutes moves it from about 47% to about 1%, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.

Across the whole model, the predicted chance is lowest at about 154 daytime minutes and higher either side, and going from 112 to 249 minutes clearly raises it, even more so if the evening charge is above 17.12 US dollars: from about 2% to about 20%, against about 4% to about 14% otherwise.

One part acts on 306 of 4000 customers, 154 of whom left, and for the typical one (a customer in Idaho with 4 customer-service calls) it raises the chance from about 16% to about 26%, a rise it does not give in West Virginia (on the training data only).

More voice-mail messages and evening minutes slightly raise it steadily, and customer-service calls slightly raise it in an uneven way, to about 3% to 6%; a voice-mail plan slightly lowers it to below 1%, and the model ignores the daytime charge, evening calls, international calls and night-time charge.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available

ann_90.text: Through this part, the model treats a higher total daytime minutes as clearly raising the predicted chance that a customer leaves steadily: for a typical customer, it goes from below 1% at 112 minutes to about 17% at 249 minutes, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted risk cannot go much lower.

Through this part, for a typical customer, the model gives a clearly higher predicted chance that a customer leaves if the customer has an international plan (about 16%) than if the customer has no international plan (about 1%).

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted value only slightly: a higher voice-mail messages raises it steadily; California (rather than any other state) raises it; Washington (rather than any other state) raises it; a higher total international charge raises it steadily; a higher total evening minutes raises it steadily; Montana (rather than any other state) raises it; a higher total evening charge raises it steadily; a voice-mail plan (rather than no voice-mail plan) lowers it; and 31 still smaller effects listed in the evidence table (on the training data only).

ann_91.text: This part acts on 3147 of 4000 training customers (79%).
For a typical customer it acts on, it slightly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 1% without this part to about 1% with it.
In the training data, 409 of these 3147 customers had churn.

A higher total daytime minutes clearly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves, and even more so if state is something other than Arkansas, New Mexico, California, South Dakota, Utah (in a curve that is lowest at about 160 minutes, higher either side for customers with state other than Arkansas, New Mexico, California, South Dakota, Utah): for a typical customer, total daytime minutes going from 112 minutes to 249 minutes moves the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 2% to about 17% if state is something other than Arkansas, New Mexico, California, South Dakota, Utah, and from about 6% to about 11% if the customer is in South Dakota.

Other effects: total daytime minutes past about 169 minutes lowers it in an uneven way; a higher total daytime minutes lowers it in an uneven way; total daytime minutes depending on total evening charge raises it in a curve that is lowest at about 154 minutes, higher either side.

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted value only slightly: customer-service calls depending on total evening charge raises it in an uneven way; total evening charge depending on state lowers it in an uneven way; total international charge past about 2.96 US dollars lowers it in an uneven way; total evening charge past about 18.05 US dollars lowers it in an uneven way; a higher total international charge lowers it in an uneven way; a higher customer-service calls raises it in an uneven way; a higher total evening charge lowers it in an uneven way; South Dakota (rather than any other state) raises it; and 3 still smaller effects listed in the evidence table (on the training data only).

ann_92.text: This part acts on 306 of 4000 training customers (8%).
For a typical customer it acts on, it raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 16% without this part to about 26% with it (on the training data only).
